justice: The street space is dominated by a wide motor-vehicle carriageway, while no dedicated sidewalk is visible on either side, indicating uneven allocation of space among road users.
Road edge lines and a centerline are clearly marked for vehicles, but there are no visible pedestrian crossings, curb ramps, or barrier-free access elements for non-motorized users.
The tree-lined edges provide some environmental benefit to all users, yet the lack of separated facilities for walking and cycling limits equitable access to the corridor.
safety: The long straight roadway provides very good forward visibility, which can help drivers detect hazards early.
There is no visible sidewalk, guardrail, or physical buffer between the travel lane and the vegetated roadside, reducing safety for pedestrians and cyclists.
Only basic lane markings are visible, while no traffic calming devices, pedestrian crossing infrastructure, or protected cycling facilities can be seen.
livability: The corridor appears isolated, with no visible shops, houses, transit stops, or community facilities that would support daily social life.
Continuous roadside trees improve environmental quality, but the space functions primarily as a through-road rather than a socially active street.
There are no visible benches, plazas, bus shelters, or gathering spaces that would support lingering or everyday public use.
sustainability: Continuous rows of mature trees on both sides contribute to shading, carbon absorption, and roadside ecological value.
The absence of visible dedicated bus infrastructure or high-quality non-motorized facilities limits support for low-carbon transport choices beyond driving.
The green roadside verge and planted edges suggest some permeable landscape area compared with a fully paved street section.
aesthetics: The symmetrical rows of trees on both sides create a strong sense of visual order and rhythm.
The roadway surface appears clean and well maintained, contributing to a neat overall appearance.
The open sky view and continuous green corridor give the street a calm, spacious scenic quality.
comfort: The roadside tree canopy likely improves thermal comfort along the edges, even though the center of the asphalt road remains highly exposed to sun.
The pavement appears smooth and even, which supports physical comfort for vehicle travel and potentially for cycling at the road edge.
Low visible traffic volume and the absence of crowding suggest relatively good psychological comfort due to a calm and uncluttered environment.
No benches, shelters, or designated resting areas are visible, reducing comfort for anyone traveling outside a vehicle.
walkability: No sidewalk is visible, so pedestrians would likely need to use the road shoulder or edge, which greatly weakens walking conditions.
There are no marked crossings, pedestrian signals, or refuge islands visible along this long corridor.
Although the road is straight and visually clear, the large paved carriageway and lack of pedestrian-oriented infrastructure make walking unattractive and inconvenient.
bikeability: There is no protected bike lane or clearly marked cycling space visible on either side of the roadway.
The smooth road surface and straight alignment may support basic riding conditions, but cyclists appear to share space directly with motor traffic.
No bicycle parking, bicycle signs, or intersection treatments for cyclists are visible, indicating weak cycling support infrastructure.
